extracted.intended_audience: college students (writers and peer reviewers) preparing or reviewing literature reviews / rhetorical analyses in writing courses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for student reviewers and writers on how to conduct and receive peer review focused on literature reviews or rhetorical analyses; includes required submission items, stepwise reviewer actions, checklist questions, and feedback structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive criticism over vague praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Peers benefit more from constructive criticism than vague praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "A comment like 'I got confused here' or 'I saw your point clearly here' are more useful than 'It looks okay to me.' Point out ways your classmates can improve their work."

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer submission requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When submitting a rough draft, include answers at the top of your draft to two questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "What questions do you have for your reviewer?" and "What two (or more) concerns do you have about your literature review?" (These items signal what the reviewer should address in Step 3.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the draft twice
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should read the peer's paper two times: once for overview, a second time for critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "First, read your peer’s rhetorical analysis two times: once to get an overview of the paper, and a second time to provide constructive criticism for the author to use when revising his/her paper."

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: presents topic and background
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the draft include an introduction that presents the topic and provides appropriate background information?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "...to clarify the context in which the writer is reviewing the literature" — check whether the introduction sets up the topic and context clearly for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization: grouping of literature by common denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: Are research studies and other types of literature grouped according to common denominators?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for meaningful grouping criteria (examples given): "qualitative versus quantitative approaches, conclusions of authors, purpose or objective, chronology." Evaluate whether groupings clarify relationships among sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-level summary and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Are all individual sources briefly summarized and analyzed, with descriptions of their strengths and weaknesses?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each source has both a concise summary and an evaluative comment (strengths/weaknesses) rather than only citation or description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source reliability and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the sources reliable? Are they varied?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess credibility (peer-reviewed, reputable publishers, methodological rigor) and diversity of source types (reviews, theoretical articles, case studies, empirical studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion: summarizes contributions and connects to discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the draft include a conclusion that summarizes the most important contributions sources make to the topic and connects these points to the larger discipline or profession?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the conclusion synthesizes key contributions and situates the literature's significance for the field or practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective note: what was most interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer should note what they found most interesting about the draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "What did you find most interesting about this draft?" — use this to highlight engaging or original elements worth keeping or developing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address writer's stated questions and concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must directly respond to the questions and concerns the writer listed at the top of the draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 3: "Address the questions and concerns your partner wrote at the top of the draft." These responses are expected and should be specific and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two short feedback paragraphs (strengths and improvements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide two brief paragraphs: first about what the writer does especially well; second about what the writer should do to improve the essay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "In the first short paragraph, write about what the writer does especially well. In the second short paragraph, write about what you think the writer should do to improve his or her essay. Your suggestions will be the most useful part of peer review for your classmates, so focus more of your time on these paragraphs; they will count for more of your peer review grade than the yes or no responses."

rubrics_metrics.name: Hints for effective peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: General best-practice guidance for giving useful peer feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these heuristics: "Point out the strengths. Address the larger issues first. Make specific suggestions for improvement. Be tactful but be candid and direct. Don’t be afraid to disagree with another reviewer. Make and receive comments in a useful way. Remember that peer review is not an editing service."
